input: In a development that will be of considerable interest to the cement industry, an amine absorption unit has been successfully tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln, demonstrating the considerable potential of this approach for industrial carbon capture. Over the course of a 90-day campaign, the unit treated 14 t of carbon dioxide per day and captured an impressive 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while solvent loss stood at just 1.6 kg per tonne captured, figures that compare favourably with expectations for this technology at this scale. It is worth noting, however, that beyond 90 days the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, and this represents an important area for future investigation. Overall, these results highlight the promise of amine absorption for kiln gas and underscore the need for longer-term testing in order to fully understand solvent behaviour over extended periods of operation. Going forward, it will be interesting to see how the technology performs when it is deployed at larger scales and over the longer campaigns that commercial operation would inevitably demand in practice.
target: An amine absorption unit at pilot scale captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in gas from a cement kiln. The unit treated 14 t of carbon dioxide per day over a 90-day campaign. Steam demand was 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne captured. Both consumption figures are stated per tonne captured rather than per tonne treated, so they scale with the captured quantity and not with the gas throughput. The capture rate and the consumption figures together define the operating cost of the process at this scale: steam sets the energy demand of the regeneration step, and solvent loss sets the make-up rate that a longer campaign would have to sustain. Neither figure is a design value; both are measured performance over the campaign as run. The gas treated was kiln gas as produced, at the composition the kiln delivered during the campaign, so the capture rate is reported for that gas and not for a cleaned or conditioned feed. The campaign establishes performance for its own duration only. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested; dust carried over with the gas may raise solvent loss or degrade capture, and neither outcome is excluded by the present data. A longer run with dust exposure monitored is the step that would extend the tested period.
